summary: Ido Pesok, an engineer at Vercel working on v0 (a full stack vibe coding platform), presents an introduction to evals at the application layer, distinguishing them from research-layer evals used by model labs. v0 recently crossed 100 million messages sent and launched GitHub sync functionality. Pesok uses a humorous example—the 'Fruit Letter Counter' app—to demonstrate AI unreliability. The app counts letters in fruit names, but despite testing successfully multiple times before shipping, users encounter failures with unexpected queries (e.g., counting Rs across a long list of fruits). This illustrates that AI apps are 'demo-savvy'—they look great in demos but hallucinate in production. Even when 95% of an app works 100% of the time, the crucial 5% can fail. Pesok introduces a basketball court analogy to visualize evals. Data (user queries) are points on the court. The task (in Braintrust terminology) is how you shoot—your system prompt, pre-processing, RAG, etc. The score checks whether the ball went in. Understanding the 'court'—your domain of user queries—is the most important step. Two traps to avoid: the out-of-bounds trap (building evals for queries users don't care about) and the concentrated-points trap (not testing across the entire domain). For data collection, Pesok recommends thumbs up/down signals, observability log sampling (100 random samples weekly), community forums, and social media. For structuring evals, he advocates keeping constants in data and variables in the task, mirroring factoring constants in math. AI SDK middleware enables sharing logic between production API routes and evals, making practice as similar as possible to the real game. For scoring, he recommends leaning toward deterministic pass/fail scoring for easier debugging and team distribution. A scoring trick involves adding output formatting tags (e.g., answer tags) to prompts to enable easy string matching during evals, even though such tags wouldn't be wanted in production. Pesok highly recommends adding evals to CI/CD using Braintrust eval reports, which show improvements and regressions across the court when colleagues make PRs that change prompts. He frames evals as practice—your model practices, and switching models is like switching players. 'Improvement without measurement is limited and imprecise,' and evals give the clarity needed to systematically improve. Benefits include better reliability and quality, higher conversion and retention, and less time on support and ops. In Q&A, Pesok recommends running evals daily or on a schedule, and acknowledges that running the same question multiple times to get a success percentage is a valid approach, especially for harder questions farther from the basket. The court diagrams themselves were built using v0.

sections.title: Introduction to Vercel's v0 and its growth
sections.summary: Ido Pesok introduces v0 as a full stack vibe coding platform, announcing GitHub sync functionality and that v0 has crossed 100 million messages sent.

sections.title: The problem with AI unreliability and the Fruit Letter Counter example
sections.summary: Pesok tells the story of the Fruit Letter Counter app to illustrate AI unreliability. Despite testing successfully before shipping, users encounter failures with unexpected queries. He explains that AI apps are demo-savvy—looking great in demos but hallucinating in production. Prompt engineering attempts (an 'exuberant fruit-loving AI' prompt tested 10 times successfully) still fail when users submit more complex queries.

sections.title: Introducing evals and the basketball court analogy
sections.summary: Pesok introduces the basketball court analogy for evals. Data (user queries) are points on the court. The task (Braintrust terminology) is how you shoot the ball. The score checks if it went in. He plots example queries on the court—easy queries near the basket, hard ones farther away, and out-of-domain queries out of bounds.

sections.title: Defining the court: understanding the domain and avoiding traps
sections.summary: Understanding the court (domain) is the most important step. Two traps to avoid: the out-of-bounds trap (building evals for queries users don't care about) and the concentrated-points trap (not testing across the entire domain). A good court visualization shows boundaries, blue/red distribution, and helps prioritize where to focus improvements.

sections.title: Data collection for evals
sections.summary: Pesok recommends collecting data from thumbs up/down signals, observability logs (sampling 100 random samples weekly), community forums, and X/Twitter. There are no shortcuts—understanding the court requires real work.

sections.title: Structuring evals: constants in data, variables in task
sections.summary: Keep constants in data (user queries that never change) and variables in the task (system prompts, pre-processing, RAG). This mirrors factoring constants in math for clarity, reuse, and generalization. AI SDK middleware enables sharing logic between production API routes and evals, making practice as similar as possible to the real game.

sections.title: Scoring evals
sections.summary: Scoring varies by domain—simple for letter counting, difficult for writing tasks. Pesok recommends leaning toward deterministic pass/fail scoring for easier debugging and team distribution. Keep scores simple. Ask 'What am I looking for to see if this failed?' and write code that checks for it. Human review is acceptable when automated scoring is too hard.

sections.title: Scoring tricks, CI/CD integration, and talk summary
sections.summary: Pesok shares a scoring trick: add output formatting tags (e.g., answer tags) to prompts during evals for easy string matching, even though such tags aren't wanted in production. He highly recommends adding evals to CI/CD using Braintrust eval reports, which show improvements and regressions across the court when PRs change prompts. Evals function as practice—switching models is like switching players. 'Improvement without measurement is limited and imprecise.' Benefits include better reliability and quality, higher conversion and retention, and less time on support and ops. The court diagrams were built using v0.

sections.title: Q&A: eval frequency and repeated runs
sections.summary: In Q&A, Pesok recommends running evals daily or on a schedule to catch regressions. He acknowledges that running the same question multiple times to get a success percentage is valid, especially as harder questions farther from the basket have lower success rates.
